haiku-low.q1: On-call starts it by running the failover command. Probes only page on-call when 2 of 3 locations see 3 failed checks; they never fail over automatically.
haiku-low.q2: The command stops, changes nothing, and releases the lock. On-call may start a new run with an explicit accept-data-loss override.
haiku-low.q3: Before promotion, A is fenced and the fencing wait ends. Before workers start, jobs are reset. Before DNS, B is scaled to 12 and passes its health check.
haiku-low.q4: B's Redis starts empty, so users signed in at failover must sign in again.
haiku-low.q5: It is never reused as primary. It is rebuilt as a replica of B, and writes that never reached B are kept for manual review.
haiku-low.q6: A's own app and worker instances refuse writes when they cannot renew their lease, since the control store names B; the lease then expires and they stop writing.
haiku-low.q7: The control store holds the active-region record. The failover command and abort write it; every app instance and worker reads and renews it through its lease check.
haiku-low.q8: Step 5 resets their rows from running to pending so B's workers pick them up. Jobs may run twice, so they must be idempotent; recent unreplicated enqueues may be lost.
haiku-low.q9: Rerun the command to resume from the first unfinished step; the lock prevents concurrent runs. Abort to A is allowed only during steps 1 to 3 while A is reachable. From step 4 on, no abort.
haiku-low.q10: Users follow the change to B within the 60 s TTL, which counts toward the RTO. What clients experience during that window is NOT STATED.
haiku-low.q11: Up to 30 s of the newest writes, the RPO. The lag check stops failover if B's replay lag is over 30 s, unless the override is used.

sonnet.q1: On-call decides and runs the failover command; failover is never automatic. Detection (2 of 3 probe locations see 3 consecutive failed /healthz checks) only pages on-call.
sonnet.q2: If B's last recorded replay lag is over 30 s, the command stops, changes nothing, and releases the lock. On-call can start a new run with an explicit accept-data-loss override, or investigate first.
sonnet.q3: Before promoting B's database: the run lock is taken, the lag check passed (or override), and A is fenced (active region set to B, epoch +1, and the wait of one lease period plus margin has finished). Before B's workers start: B's database is promoted and writable, running jobs are reset to pending, and B's web/API tier is scaled up to 12. Before DNS points at B: B is scaled up and passes its health check.
sonnet.q4: Sessions are lost. B's Redis starts empty (not replicated), so everyone signed in must sign in again; this is accepted.
sonnet.q5: It is never reused as primary. It is rebuilt as a replica of B, and any writes it held that never reached B are kept for manual review. Moving back to A is a separate, planned switchover, never automatic.
sonnet.q6: A's own code fails closed. Instances and workers may write only while their lease is valid and the control-store record names their region as active. They cannot renew once the record says B (or the store is unreachable), so they stop writing when the lease expires. The command waits one lease period plus margin before promoting B.
sonnet.q7: The control store (a small strongly consistent key-value store outside Region A) holds the active-region record (e.g. {active_region, epoch}). The failover command writes it (sets active region = B, epoch+1; abort sets it back to A with higher epoch). App instances and workers read it to renew their leases.
sonnet.q8: Step 5 resets every row left 'running' on B to 'pending', so B's workers pick them up. Those jobs may run twice, so every job must be safe to repeat (e.g. idempotency keys). Jobs enqueued in the last seconds before A was lost may not have reached B and are lost, which is accepted within the RPO.
sonnet.q9: Rerunning the command resumes from the first unfinished step, since each step is recorded in the run record and is safe to repeat; the lock prevents concurrent runs. Going back to A (abort) is possible only during steps 1 to 3 (nothing promoted), and abort is refused if A is still unreachable, in which case on-call resumes the failover. From step 4 on there is no abort.
sonnet.q10: NOT STATED. The document says only that the DNS name has a 60 s TTL, users follow the change within that TTL, and A's apps refuse writes once fenced; it does not describe what a client with a stale cached answer experiences.
sonnet.q11: Up to the RPO of 30 s of the newest writes. The limit is enforced by the lag check: if B's last recorded replay lag is over 30 s, the command stops unless on-call uses the accept-data-loss override, which accepts losing more than the RPO. The replication is asynchronous, and the lag is usually under 5 s.
